headline: Harvest Moon Tide Turns Penobscot Bay: Pollock Wake Up, Bass Thin Out, Mackerel Push Through
subhead: Big tides moved bait hard this week — the bass bite is fading right on schedule, but pollock and mackerel are stepping into the gap.
body_markdown:
Old Stonington hands have a saying about the Harvest Moon tide — it doesn't ask, it tells. Forty years of reading that current push through Penobscot Bay has taught me it moves bait first and fish second, and that's exactly what it did this week. The bigger swings off the full moon dragged water through the Bay's channels with real authority, stacking bait against ledges and river mouths and forcing every predator in the system to commit to a feeding window instead of loafing through the tide. That's the kind of week that separates the boats that time it right from the ones that show up an hour late.

Water's cooling steadily now, upper 50s in the open Bay and holding a touch warmer in the protected coves off Boothbay and up into the St. George and Damariscotta rivers. That's the number that matters most right now. We flagged it a week back — said striper action would keep going but start easing off as temperatures kept sliding — and that's precisely what the fleet is seeing. Bass haven't left the building, but the numbers are down from two weeks ago and the fish that remain are bunched tighter to structure and feeding in shorter windows, mostly the last two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the flood at first light.

The better bass action right now is in the river mouths — Medomak, St. George, and the upper reaches of the Damariscotta — where warmer, bait-rich water is still funneling out on the ebb. Fish are holding on the drop-offs where the river current meets the Bay, and they're eating small profile baits: three- to four-inch white or chartreuse soft plastics on light jig heads, and bunker-imitation plugs like a small Doc or a slim darter worked over the seam at first light. Nothing oversized this week — mostly schoolies to low twenties, with the occasional better fish mixed in around the deeper bends where the current stacks bait against a ledge. If you're chasing bass over the next few days, fish the top of the ebb and be gone by mid-morning. The window's shrinking, not opening.

Mackerel are the story filling the gap, and they're pushing hard right now off Boothbay and around the outer islands. Birds are working bait balls off the Cuckolds and around Ram Island, and mackerel trees or small Diamond jigs dropped through the school will load up fast — good for the smoker and good bait for anyone rigging live or fresh-cut for bigger fish. That mackerel push is exactly what you want to see this time of year; it's the leading edge of the fall forage shift, and it's dragging pollock and the last of the bass activity along behind it.

Pollock have turned on at Monhegan, and that's worth the run if the weather cooperates. Schoolie pollock are chasing bait on the surface in the last hour of daylight around the back side ledges and out toward Eastern Egg Rock, showing themselves in nervous water and diving birds the same way the mackerel do. One- to two-ounce diamond jigs or soft plastic shads worked with a fast retrieat and a pause will draw strikes right at the surface — no need to go deep when they're up chasing bait like this. Whitehead Island, off Spruce Head, has been holding a similar pattern on calmer evenings, smaller fish but a reliable bend in the rod for anyone who wants an easy Bay-side outing without running all the way to Monhegan.

Groundfish remain the steady, unglamorous backbone of this fishery, and this week hasn't changed that. Cod and haddock are still holding in the deeper channels of Penobscot Bay, particularly the water running between Vinalhaven and Isle au Haut, where depths push 120 to 180 feet and the bottom stays cold and stable through the season. The bigger tides this week made those channels tougher to fish — more current means heavier jigs, and slack water around the tide change is still the most efficient time to get a bait down clean instead of fighting the sweep. Diamond jigs tipped with clam or a bottom rig baited with fresh herring have both been producing, mostly keeper-class haddock with the occasional cod mixed in. Deer Isle and Stonington boats working those same channels are seeing similar results — steady, not spectacular, but dependable if you fish the tide correctly instead of against it.

Looking at the next several days, expect the pattern to hold its shape rather than flip. Striper numbers should keep easing as the water keeps dropping through the upper 50s into the fifties proper — that migration south is a one-way street this time of year, and the fish still in the Bay will keep concentrating in river mouths and warmer pockets before they push out. Mackerel and pollock should stay active and likely build over the next week as more bait gets pushed through on these bigger tides, particularly around Monhegan and the outer islands where the water stays cleaner and colder longer. Watch the wind — a stiff northeast blow would dirty up the nearshore water and could shut down the surface pollock bite faster than the calendar will. Groundfish in the deep Penobscot Bay channels should stay steady regardless of surface conditions, which makes that the safer bet if the weather turns unsettled toward the weekend.
